text: The second sūkta, beginning इंद्र त्वा (*iṃdra tvā*), nine Ṛks, is Vaiśvāmitra (seer Viśvāmitra), its metre Gāyatrī, its deity Indra. The Anukramaṇī agrees: इंद्र त्वा गायत्रं हीति (*iṃdra tvā gāyatraṃ hīti*). In the Agniṣṭoma, at the morning pressing, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin recites this sūkta as his śastra. The sūtra says: इंद्र त्वा वृषभमुद्देवभीति तिस्रः (*iṃdra tvā vṛṣabhamuddevabhīti tisraḥ*) (Ā. Sū. 5-10). The first Ṛk is the prasthita-yājyā of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin at the morning pressing; the sūtra says: इंद्र त्वा वृषभं मरुतो यस्य (*iṃdra tvā vṛṣabhaṃ maruto yasya*) (Ā. Sū. 5-5).⟨NOTE:6⟩

text: (8) इांइंधी दीप्ताविति धातुः । भूतानि प्राणिदेहानिंदे जीवचैतन्यरूपेणांतःप्रविश्य दीपयतीतींद्रः ॥ (*iāṃiṃdhī dīptāviti dhātuḥ | bhūtāni prāṇidehāniṃde jīvacaitanyarūpeṇāṃtaḥpraviśya dīpayatītīṃdraḥ ‖*)⟨NOTE:7⟩ The root indh means to shine, to illumine. Entering the bodies of living beings in the form of the life-force, and shining while impelling them to do their respective acts; therefore the name Indra.

text: (11) औपम्यनवनामको मुनिरिदंदर्शनादिंद्र इति निर्वचनवाह । इदमित्यापरोक्ष्यमुच्यते । (*aupamyanavanāmako muniridaṃdarśanādiṃdra iti nirvacanavāha | idamityāparokṣyamucyate |*)⟨NOTE:9⟩—The sage Aupamanyava says that because he sees this, that is, everything, the name Indra arose. Here "this" means the imperceptible, what does not appear visibly to the eye. For that very reason the Śruti says परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः (*parokṣapriyā iva hi devāḥ*).

text: (13) इनशब्दस्येश्वरवाचकस्याकारलोपे सति नकारांतमिन्निति पदं भवति । द्य भय इति धातुः । स च परमेश्वरः शत्रूणां दारयिता भीषयितेतींद्रः ॥ (*inaśabdasyeśvaravācakasyākāralope sati nakārāṃtaminniti padaṃ bhavati | dya bhaya iti dhātuḥ | sa ca parameśvaraḥ śatrūṇāṃ dārayitā bhīṣayitetīṃdraḥ ‖*)—The word ina denotes the Lord. If the vowel a over the n of this word ina is dropped, the word in remains. The root dṛ⟨NOTE:10⟩ means fear. That god, the Supreme Lord, causes fear to enemies; hence the name Indra.

text: पिब (*piba*)—The final syllable of this word is made long in the Saṃhitā text for the convenience of the metre. Such usage is frequent in the Ṛgveda. For example, the word पिब (*piba*) in पिबा सोममभि (*pibā somamabhi*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-17-1); पिबा सोममिंद्र मंदतु (*pibā somamiṃdra maṃdatu*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-22-1); पिबा सोमं मदाय (*pibā somaṃ madāya*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-95-3); पिबा सोमं महते (*pibā somaṃ mahate*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-116-1); the verse ⟨NOTE:11⟩

text: वृषस्व (*vṛṣasva*)—जठरे सिंच । यथा नाभेरधो न पतति तथा धारयेति भावः । (*jaṭhare siṃca | yathā nābheradho na patati tathā dhārayeti bhāvaḥ |*) In this verse it is plainly said पिब (*piba*), "drink the Soma juice"; is not the use of the word वृषस्व (*vṛṣasva*) then useless? The answer: since Indra is famous as extremely fond of drinking Soma juice, the use of the two words पिब (*piba*) and वृषभ (*vṛṣabha*) ⟨NOTE:12⟩ is also proper, to stress plainly: "when drinking Soma, drink as much as you wish, so that it does not fall below the navel, and drink so that the inner part of the belly is well soaked and refreshed."

text: धृतस्नू (*dhṛtasnū*)—श्रमजनितजलप्रस्रवणयुक्तौ (*śramajanitajalaprasravaṇayuktau*). Since the word dhṛta is read among the names of water (Ni. 2-24), dhṛta means water, the water of exertion, that is, sweat. Because horses run fast over a long distance, their bodies are soaked with sweat. In the same way here, because Indra's horses have brought Indra from far away to our place of sacrifice, their bodies are drenched with sweat. That condition is described here by the word धृतस्नू (*dhṛtasnū*). ⟨NOTE:19⟩

text: Sāyaṇa addresses Indra: "O Indra, pass beyond all the peoples (चर्षणीः (*carṣaṇīḥ*) = prajāḥ) and come to us." Aryaḥ means our lord. "Our prayers (आशिषः (*āśiṣaḥ*)) are of this kind: 'Come here and drink the Soma'. Accepting them, come to us yoked with your two horses." Further, these hymns (मतयः (*matayaḥ*), praises), fashioned by the praisers, desiring your friendship, invoke you for the drinking of Soma. हि (*hi*) is the well-known particle. The action of the doer is attributed to the instrument, as in "the firewood cooks". ⟨NOTE:26⟩

text: "O Indra, make me, many times (कुवित् (*kuvit*)), the protector (गोपां (*gopāṃ*)) of the people. O wealthy (मघवन् (*maghavan*)), Soma-possessing Indra, make me king, the lord of all. Make me also a ऋषिं (*ṛṣiṃ*), a questioner of supersensuous matters; "a seer from seeing", says Yāska. Make me also a drinker (पपिवांसं (*papivāṃsaṃ*)) of the pressed Soma. And give me imperishable wealth (अमृतस्य (*amṛtasya*) वस्वः (*vasvaḥ*)). शिक्षाः (*śikṣāḥ*) means 'give'; the root शिक्षति (*śikṣati*) has the sense of giving." ⟨NOTE:27⟩

text: Mūrāḥ: for the word mūra the meaning "foolish" (mūḍha), i.e. ignorant, is generally well known; mūra is popularly an ignorant person and amūra a knowing one. In the present Ṛk, however, Sāyaṇa explains the word as a destroying power. The scholar Monier Wiliam, explaining this word, cites this very Ṛk and in his dictionary gives the meaning "Rushing, impetuous"; he also records Sāyaṇa's opinion "destroyer" (māraka). Besides, it also means "firm, secure, well established". The word is also used in the sense of "root, base" (A. Ve. 1-28-3).⟨NOTE:28⟩

text: As the words of the Supreme Person say, उत्तीदेयुरिमे लोकाः न कुर्यां कर्म चेदहं (*uttīdeyurime lokāḥ na kuryāṃ karma cedahaṃ*)⟨NOTE:29⟩—"if I did not perform action, all the worlds would perish"—so, if Indra, the lord of the universe, were not constantly engaged in action useful for the conduct of the world, the ruin of the world would be certain. He is the cause of the appearance of Dawn and of the rising of the sun. As described in स्वराजः, महतः, ते (*svarājaḥ, mahataḥ, te*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-46-1), he alone is lord of the whole universe and holds sovereign rank. Even so, because the performance of sacrifice nourishes the world and is the cause of the growth of prosperity of the whole world, of gods, men and others, it is said that Indra honoured Dawn and the Sun, the primary causes of that sacrifice. The purport of the present Ṛk is that, though himself the lord, he worshipped his own creation, which nourishes the world.

text: Here, in वृधस्य दक्षसः विदे (*vṛdhasya dakṣasaḥ vide*), it is stated that in order to acquire strength that makes one grow, Indra purifies the sacrificer (his resolve), as in क्रतुं पुनीते (*kratuṃ punīte*). Even when the person's spiritual aim is explained, it is set out in sentences such as ओं क्रतो स्मर (*oṃ krato smara*) (Īśa. 17) ⟨NOTE:31⟩ and क्रतुमयःपुरुषः (*kratumayaḥpuruṣaḥ*) (Chā. U. 3-14-2). In such contexts Śaṅkarācārya has explained the word क्रतु (*kratu*) as resolution, or as the person's duty; the purport is resolve, and the power of action that accomplishes the resolve. According to this resolve and power the aim is accomplished. The nature of क्रतु (*kratu*) is stated thus: यथाक्रतुरस्मिल्लोके पुरुषो भवति तथेतः प्रेत्य भवति स क्रतुं कुर्वीत (*yathākraturasmilloke puruṣo bhavati tathetaḥ pretya bhavati sa kratuṃ kurvīta*) and so on. In the present Ṛk too the nature of the wealth that comes to such a person made of क्रतु (*kratu*) is described.

text: महिष (*mahiṣa*)—The word mahiṣa is read among the names for "great" in the Nirukta (Ni. 3-3). It means venerable, or else the accomplisher of great deeds. The Nirukta-author quotes the ṛk "अपामुपस्थे महिषा... (*apāmupasthe mahiṣā...*)" (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-8-4) and there explains this word as "deep". The intention here is that Indra's personal power is deep. In this power there is a blending of both beauty and terror(?). ⟨NOTE:33⟩For that reason the epithet उग्र (*ugra*) is fitting. Hence, without giving here the meaning "sprinkler" for the word वृष्णेभिः (*vṛṣṇebhiḥ*), it is shown that it is used in the sense of "power": वृष्णेभिः (*vṛṣṇebhiḥ*) means "by powers that accomplish great deeds".

text: Indra, shining, not fully known by all ("this much is his power"), the Soma-possessor, has surpassed the मात्राः (*mātrāḥ*). These are things that are measured and bounded, namely rock-heaps (शिलोच्चयाः (*śiloccayāḥ*)); he has exceeded even these, becoming greatly excessive. Likewise he has surpassed even the gods by मज्जना (*majjanā*), that is by strength: majja is strength, because it plunges (मज्जयति (*majjayati*)) into the face of the sea of enemies. By that strength he has surpassed; so too heaven and earth, and the vast, great firmament. The rest of the block gives derivations and accent notes (mātrābhiḥ, rocamānaḥ, apratītaḥ, majjanā, pṛthivyāḥ). ⟨NOTE:34⟩

notes.question: ಯಜೀಷೀ in the Sanskrit block against ಋಜೀಷೀ in the Kannada Pratipadārtha and pada text; read ṛjīṣī

text: मात्राभिः (*mātrābhiḥ*)—As explained earlier in Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-38-3, here too it is explained: "मीयंते मांतीति वा मात्रा: शिलोच्चयाः (*mīyaṃte māṃtīti vā mātrā: śiloccayāḥ*)". It is formed from the root mā, meaning "to measure". Although it applies to all things possessing limit, here it is explained as lofty rock-heaps. When describing the nature of all the elements such as earth, the Upaniṣads use this word thus: "पृथिवी च पृथिवीमात्रा चापश्चापोमात्राच तेजश्चतेजोमात्रा च वायुश्च नायुमात्रा च आकाशश्चाकाशमात्रा ॥ (*pṛthivī ca pṛthivīmātrā cāpaścāpomātrāca tejaścatejomātrā ca vāyuśca nāyumātrā ca ākāśaścākāśamātrā ‖*)" (Praśne. 4-8). ⟨NOTE:35⟩ In the quoted sentence the word mātrā has the technical meaning tanmātra ("subtle element"). Here there is no room for a philosophical discussion; in sum, they may be called things confined to the limits of man. The intention is that Indra has grown beyond all these.

text: ऋजीषी (*ṛjīṣī*)—This epithet is because he is accompanied by Soma. It is used chiefly in describing the nature of Indra and the Maruts. In such contexts as "अमत्रेभिर्यजीषिणिमिंद्रं (*amatrebhiryajīṣiṇimiṃdraṃ*)" (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-42-2) ⟨NOTE:36⟩ the word ṛjīṣa is explained as power; it is explained as "of Indra, who has obtained power that obstructs enemies". But in many contexts this epithet is well known precisely because he is accompanied by Soma.

text: The Ṛk ये त्वाहिहत्ये (*ye tvāhihatye*) is the yājyā in the Marutvatīya śastra. It is prescribed by the sūtra ये त्वाहिहत्ये मघवन्नवर्धन्निति याज्या (*ye tvāhihatye maghavannavardhanniti yājyā*) (Ā. 5-14). O Maghavan Indra, the Maruts who in the work of slaying Ahi (Vṛtra) strengthened you by giving you strength, with words such as "strike, blessed one, slay, show your valour"; and, O Harivān (possessor of horses) Indra, those who strengthened you in the battle connected with the slaying of Śambara. That Indra slew Śambara is stated by a mantra passage: यः शंबरं पर्वतेषु क्षियंतं चत्वारिंश्यां शरद्यन्वविंदत् । ओजायमानं यो अहिं जघान । (*yaḥ śaṃbaraṃ parvateṣu kṣiyaṃtaṃ catvāriṃśyāṃ śaradyanvaviṃdat | ojāyamānaṃ yo ahiṃ jaghāna |*) (Ṛgve. 2-12-11)⟨NOTE:39⟩. Likewise the Maruts who strengthened you in the battle for cattle, गविष्टौ (*gaviṣṭau*), against the asuras named Paṇis; and the wise

text: That this Ṛk beginning ये त्वाहिहत्ये (*ye tvāhihatye*) is to be recited as the yājyā mantra at the time of reciting the Marutvatīya śastra is explained by the sūkta⟨NOTE:40⟩ of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta-sūtra, ये त्वाहिहत्ये मघवन्नवर्धन्निति याज्या (*ye tvāhihatye maghavannavardhanniti yājyā*) (Ā. 5-14).

text: "O Indra, मरुत्वंतं (*marutvaṃtaṃ*)", accompanied by the Maruts; वृषभं (*vṛṣabhaṃ*), the rainer of waters by splitting the cloud; ववृधानं (*vavṛdhānaṃ*), growing through zeal in works such as the slaying of Vṛtra; akavāri, one who has many enemies⟨NOTE:41⟩; "or else" — the block breaks off here and the next window continues it.

text: The block opens by completing the explanation of अकवारिं (*akavāriṃ*) begun on the previous page.⟨NOTE:42⟩ A mantra is cited in support: स्वरिरमत्तो ववक्षे रणाय (*svariramatto vavakṣe raṇāya*) (Ṛgve. 1-61-9).⟨NOTE:43⟩ Then he glosses the remaining words. दिव्यं (*divyaṃ*): dwelling in heaven. शासं (*śāsaṃ*): the ruler who governs by beneficial instruction and by warding off harm. विश्वासाहं (*viśvāsāhaṃ*): the overcomer of every adversary. उग्रं (*ugraṃ*): formidable against enemies. सहोदां (*sahodāṃ*): the giver of strength to the Maruts, his allies in battle. Indra, so endowed, we call to this rite for new, that is, fresher protection (नूतनाय (*nūtanāya*), अवसे (*avase*), हुवेम (*huvema*): "we invoke you"). The rest of the block is grammar on नूतनाय (*nūtanāya*).
